In 1995, Congress—reacting to concerns that class action securities lawsuits had become abusive—enacted (over a Presidential veto) the Private
Securities Litigation Reform Act (PSLRA) of 1995. The PSLRA imposed what Professor Miller has called a “super-heightened pleading standard” on
complaints brought under the 1934 Act. See Miller, The Pretrial Rush to Judgment: Are the “Litigation Explosion,” “Liability Crisis,” and Efficiency
Clichés Eroding Our Day in Court and Jury Trial Commitments?, 78 N.Y.U.L.Rev. 982, 1012 (2003). The pleader must specify every statement
alleged to have been misleading and to provide reasons that the statement is misleading. Facts giving rise to a “strong inference” that defendant acted
with the required state of mind must be stated with particularity. Moreover, if an allegation is made on information and belief, the pleader must provide
all facts on which the belief is based and state those facts with particularity. The PSLRA stays discovery while a motion to dismiss is pending,
providing a limited exception for “particularized discovery” if necessary “to preserve evidence or to prevent undue prejudice.” 15 U.S.C.
§ 78u–4(b)(3)(B). See Perino, Did the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act Work?, 2003 U.Ill.L.Rev. 913, 918–23.
One issue that divided the lower courts was the pleading of “loss causation”—whether defendant’s fraud caused plaintiff’s economic loss. In
DURA PHARMACEUTICALS, INC. v. BROUDO, 544 U.S. 336, 125 S.Ct. 1627, 161 L.Ed.2d 577 (2005), the Court rejected the Ninth Circuit’s
approach that loss causation could be sufficiently alleged by stating that “the price” of the security “on the date of purchase was inflated because of the
misrepresentation.” Instead, the pleader must allege and prove a market decline that is attributable to the fraud. Some commentators criticized the
Court’s approach as effectively converting the 1934 Securities Act into an ex post rule of immunity that is at odds with the statute’s requirement of ex
ante disclosure. See Spindler, Why Shareholders Want Their CEOs To Lie More After Dura Pharmaceuticals, 95 Geo.L.J. 653, 657, 691 (2007).
Another question that divided the courts concerned how a pleader could show the “strong inference” required under the PSLRA, a term that Congress
did not define.
